posts.hook: 876 conversations started from ads, across nine Meta ad accounts. That number sounds like a win. But a conversation is not a sale, and most posts stop right there.
posts.body:
876 conversations started from ads, across nine Meta ad accounts.

That number sounds like a win. But a conversation is not a sale, and most posts stop right there.

We looked at what separated the ones that turned into real work from the ones that went quiet.

It wasn't the reach. Total reach crossed 1.36 million people across those accounts, and reach alone told us nothing about who replied.

It wasn't even the lead count. 7,341 people filled a form across nine accounts, and plenty of those never became a conversation at all.

The pattern was in what the ad asked for before someone clicked.

Say a UK apparel campaign states a 200-piece minimum order right on the form. 19 buyers still responded, for under $6 an enquiry each. Every one of them already knew the minimum before they said hello.

Compare that to a form that only asks for a name and number. It fills up fast, and most of that fast fill-up goes cold within a week.

The forms that pre-qualify feel slower to fill. They convert to real conversations at a much higher rate.

If you're running a lead form this week, add one line that filters: budget, quantity, timeline, anything true to your business. Fewer leads, more conversations.

I put together a short audit checklist for reading your own lead-form numbers in Ads Manager. Happy to share it if it helps.

#advertising #leadgeneration #metaads

UNVERIFIED: "The pattern was in what the ad asked for before someone clicked." — States a discovered 'pattern' as fact without any approved data supporting this causal finding.

UNVERIFIED: "Compare that to a form that only asks for a name and number. It fills up fast, and most of that fast fill-up goes cold within a week." — Invented specific claim (goes cold within a week) about form performance not in approved facts.

UNVERIFIED: "The forms that pre-qualify feel slower to fill. They convert to real conversations at a much higher rate." — Presents an unverified comparative conversion-rate claim as established fact from his work.
UNVERIFIED: "Fast fill-ups go quiet fast too. The conversation dies before it starts." — Invented first-hand-sounding claim about outcome of fast-filling forms with no supporting data.
UNVERIFIED: "The forms that filtered hardest had the highest share of real conversations, not the most leads." — States a specific comparative finding as fact without approved data to support it.
check: "Some forms just ask for a name and number. They fill up fast." — Generalized claim about form fill speed presented as observed fact, not supported by approved facts.
